name: Palazzo Parisio
architectural_style: A palace rebuilt in 1900–1906 by a team of Italian architects and craftsmen that included Annibale Lupi and Carlo Sada, with an Art Nouveau façade and an interior and garden decorated in a Sicilian Baroque style, with ceiling frescoes by Giacomo Olzai and Filippo Fortunato Venuti; the grounds are laid out as formal Italian gardens

opening_hours.seasonal_note: The palazzo is open Tuesday to Sunday and closed on Mondays. Its official website does not publish opening times, so check them before you travel. It also closes to the public on some days for private events and weddings, so confirm on the day you plan to visit. The garden may remain accessible when the state rooms are reserved for private events; call ahead to confirm.

best_season: October to May — Malta summers (July–August) are very hot; the formal garden is most attractive in spring flowers; the palace interior is year-round
accessibility: The ground-floor state rooms and garden are accessible to visitors with limited mobility. The grand marble staircase leads to upper floors; step-free access to the upper rooms is not available.
tagline: A Belle Époque aristocratic palace in Naxxar — Malta's finest private residence, with a grand ballroom, frescoed ceilings, and a formal baroque garden open to the public
highlights: The ballroom and frescoed ceilings — the interior was decorated in a Sicilian Baroque style, with ceiling frescoes by Giacomo Olzai and Filippo Fortunato Venuti and gilded mouldings
The marble staircase — the entrance sequence to the state rooms; the marble work was carried out by Sicilian craftsmen in 1902
The formal Italian gardens — decorated in the same 1900–1906 campaign as the palace and open to visitors together with the state rooms

A palace rebuilt in 1900–1906 — by a team of Italian architects and craftsmen that included Annibale Lupi and Carlo Sada, with an Art Nouveau façade, for Marquis Giuseppe Scicluna, who bought the property in 1898; it has been described as “a miniature Versailles”

Wartime and film history — the wine cellar beneath the palace, now the Taverna del Marchese, served as a shelter and underground hospital during the Second World War, and the palace has appeared in Cutthroat Island and The Count of Monte Cristo (2002)
Naxxar setting — the palace stands on Victory Square (Pjazza Vittorja) in Naxxar, about 7 km west of Valletta in a straight line
description:
Palazzo Parisio stands in Naxxar, in central Malta, about 7 km west of Valletta in a straight line. The site goes back to 1733, when Grand Master António Manoel de Vilhena built a hunting lodge there. After his death it passed to the Order of St John and later to the Parisio family, who used it as a summer residence and then as the permanent home of Paolo Parisio Muscati.

The palace seen today dates from 1900–1906. Marquis Giuseppe Scicluna bought the property on 12 June 1898 and had it rebuilt by a team of Italian architects and craftsmen that included Annibale Lupi and Carlo Sada, with an Art Nouveau façade and an interior and garden decorated in a Sicilian Baroque style. The ceiling frescoes are by Giacomo Olzai and Filippo Fortunato Venuti, and Sicilian craftsmen carried out the marble work in 1902. It has been described as “a miniature Versailles”.

The visit takes in the marble staircase, the gilded ballroom with its frescoed ceiling, and the salons, dining rooms and reception halls beyond, followed by the formal Italian gardens. A self-guided visit of the state rooms and gardens takes about one to one and a half hours.

The palace and gardens are open to the public and are also used as a wedding and event venue, still owned by the Scicluna family. The palace is open Tuesday to Sunday and closed on Mondays, but private events can close it to the public on other days too, so check before you go. It has a restaurant, Luna, and serves afternoon tea, and it has appeared as a film location in Cutthroat Island and The Count of Monte Cristo (2002).
history:
In 1733 Grand Master António Manoel de Vilhena built a hunting lodge on the site. After his death it passed to the Order of St John and later to the Parisio family, who used it as a summer residence and then as the permanent home of Paolo Parisio Muscati. In 1798 it was briefly used by the French during their occupation of Malta, and in 1856 it passed to the Micallef family, who rented it to the Jesuits as a college from 1880.

On 12 June 1898 the property was bought by Marquis Giuseppe Scicluna. Between 1900 and 1906 it was rebuilt by a team of Italian architects and craftsmen that included Annibale Lupi and Carlo Sada, with an Art Nouveau façade and an interior and garden decorated in a Sicilian Baroque style; the ceiling frescoes are by Giacomo Olzai and Filippo Fortunato Venuti, and Sicilian craftsmen did the marble work in 1902. The family moved in in 1906 and the marquis died in February 1907; the family later returned to their earlier residence.

During the two world wars the palace was handed to the British government for public use, including as an RAF office, and the wine cellar beneath it, now the Taverna del Marchese, served as a shelter and underground hospital during the Second World War. The palace and gardens are now open to the public and used as a wedding and event venue, and the Scicluna family still owns them. It is scheduled as a Grade 1 property, and it has appeared as a film location in Cutthroat Island and The Count of Monte Cristo (2002).
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** Buses from Valletta serve Naxxar (approximately 30 minutes). By car from Valletta, Naxxar is approximately 10 kilometres away via the Regional Road; parking is available at the Trade Fair car park, about a five-minute walk away. From St Julian's or Sliema, bus routes connecting through the Birkirkara area serve Naxxar in approximately 25 minutes.

**Tickets:** You can buy tickets at the palace on the day, or book online in advance through the GetYourGuide link on this page (adult tickets from around €15, with instant confirmation; check the cancellation terms on the booking page). Booking online is optional. Tickets cover the palace state rooms and the gardens. The official website does not publish prices or opening times, so check the current price and hours before you go, and note that the palace is a private event venue and may be closed on a given day.

**Practical tips:** The palazzo is closed on Mondays. Arrive in the morning to maximise the chance of seeing both the state rooms and the garden before any afternoon event closures. The garden is at its best from March to May when spring planting is in colour; the palace interiors can be visited year-round when open. Malta summers (July–August) are intensely hot, so in high season the morning slot significantly reduces the midday heat in the open garden. The palace has a restaurant, Luna, and serves afternoon tea; reservations are made through palazzoparisio.com, the official website.

**Combine with:** [Mdina](/castles/malta/mdina), the medieval walled city about 5 km to the south-west of Naxxar and the original capital of Malta, reachable by car in 15 minutes or by bus via Birkirkara; and the [Grand Master's Palace](/castles/malta/grand-masters-palace) in Valletta, the palace of the Grand Masters of the Order of St John, about 6.5 km to the east.

faqs.question: What are Palazzo Parisio's opening hours?
faqs.answer: Palazzo Parisio is open Tuesday to Sunday and closed on Mondays. Its official website does not publish opening times, so check them before you travel. Allow about one to one and a half hours for the palace and gardens. The palace also closes to the public on some days for private events and weddings, so confirm before you go; the official website lists the phone number +356 21 412 461 and the email info@palazzoparisio.com.

faqs.question: How much is the Palazzo Parisio entrance fee?
faqs.answer: Adult tickets are around €15 when booked online through the GetYourGuide link on this page, and they cover the palace state rooms and the gardens. You can also buy tickets at the palace on the day, so booking online is optional; booking ahead gives instant confirmation; check the cancellation terms on the booking page. The official website does not publish prices, so check the current adult and child prices before you go.

faqs.question: Can you visit Palazzo Parisio without a guided tour?
faqs.answer: Yes. The visit is self-guided: you explore the state rooms and gardens at your own pace, and the official website offers an audio guide in six languages (English, Maltese, French, Italian, Spanish and German). The website also mentions tours of the house and gardens, so ask at the palace whether a guided tour is running on the day.

faqs.question: Is Palazzo Parisio ever closed for events?
faqs.answer: Yes. The palace is a wedding and event venue and closes to the public on some days for private events; the official website and social media have announced such closures in advance. Check before you travel by phone (+356 21 412 461) or email (info@palazzoparisio.com), as the website does not publish a visiting calendar.

faqs.question: Is the garden open separately from the palace state rooms?
faqs.answer: On days when the state rooms are reserved for a private function, the formal garden may remain accessible. In practice, access to the garden independently of the palace varies by event; call the palazzo directly to confirm. The garden visit alone, with the formal Italian gardens, takes approximately 30–40 minutes, and spring planting runs from March to May.

faqs.question: How does Palazzo Parisio fit with other historic sites in Malta?
faqs.answer: It is a palace rebuilt in 1900–1906 for a Maltese marquis, a different kind of site from the Grand Master's Palace in Valletta, the Order of St John's seat of government, and from the medieval walled city of Mdina. Mdina is about 5 km to the south-west and the Grand Master's Palace about 6.5 km to the east, so all three fit on the same route between Valletta, Naxxar and Mdina.
